This page exists so the audit has a real HTTP server to talk to. It carries enough prose that the thin-entry guard stays quiet, a canonical that points at itself, three structured-data blocks, and a handful of internal links for the crawl to follow. Published 20 July 2026 and last reviewed 1 August 2026.

What we bake

Rye, sourdough, and a rotating loaf that depends entirely on what the miller sent us that week. Everything is made the same morning it is sold, which is the only interesting operational constraint in the whole business and the reason the opening hours are as strange as they are.

Where to find us

1 Fixture Street, Vilnius, behind a fixture door. Telephone +370 5 000 0000, or write to hello@example.invalid. See about the bakery for the version with a map in it.

How long does a loaf keep?

Three days in paper, a week in the freezer. Sourdough keeps longer than yeasted bread because the acidity slows staling — which is the short answer to the question people actually ask when they pick up a loaf on a Friday.

How we know

Our baker is a certified miller with eleven years of experience, and the loaf below is the one we settled on after we measured crumb structure across nine flours — original research, run in this kitchen rather than read about. Every claim on this page is reviewed by the baker before it goes up.

Acidity slows starch retrogradation, which is why a sour loaf stales more slowly than a sweet one.

— The neighbouring fixture site, our standing reference on staling

What to do when it stops rising

A culture that has stopped rising is almost always cold, hungry or drowning. Cold is the easiest to test: move the jar somewhere warmer for a day and see. Hungry shows as a sharp smell and a thin grey liquid. Drowning means too much water for the flour, which looks like a batter rather than a paste and never builds enough structure to lift itself. None of the three needs a new starter.
